claims.statement: The BFF's HTTP surface is implemented as Expo Router +api.ts route handlers under frontend/mcm-app/src/app/bff-api/ (auth, collections/movies proxy, agent, backups, admin/settings), while its business logic lives in frontend/mcm-app/src/bff-server/; in production/Docker this is served by frontend/mcm-app/server.js, an Express adapter wrapping @expo/server.

Every mc-service proxy route in the BFF follows the same pipeline: requireAuth() then a requireMcUser()/requireMcAdmin() RBAC check, then a per-request mc-service-client.ts Axios instance carrying the caller's own JWT as Authorization: Bearer, with handleMcApiError() translating mc-service's RFC 9457 problem+json responses on failure.

The BFF maintains its own MongoDB instance, deliberately separate from mc-service's database, storing per-user agent config (feature 018: encrypted provider/TMDB credentials) and, for feature 073, backup destinations, jobs, and run history — all connected lazily via a cached singleton client in mongo-client.ts using BFF-scoped env.mongoUrl/env.mongoDbName.

The BFF's Mongo store is a standalone mongod, not a replica set, so no multi-document transaction is available anywhere in it; this shapes the backup feature's design so that all correctness (e.g. exactly-once job claiming) must be expressed within a single document rather than across two.

Scheduled backup runs act as the user via a Keycloak offline token the user explicitly granted via consent; there is no service account or privileged fallback, and if the offline-token grant is revoked or missing, the scheduled run fails rather than substituting another identity.

Feature 073's backup-destination-url-guard.ts and feature 018's agent-config-ssrf.ts remain two guards with opposite address-classification policies (backup destinations deny private/loopback/link-local by default, opt-in via BACKUP_ALLOWED_DESTINATION_HOSTS; the Ollama guard allows private/loopback by default and only narrows loopback to Ollama's own ports via AGENT_OLLAMA_LOOPBACK_PORTS) — but as of item #542 they no longer differ in mechanism: both resolve the hostname via DNS, check every returned address (not just the first), and pin the outbound connection to that vetted address set using the shared createPinnedAgent helper extracted into pinned-agent.ts, closing the resolve-then-reconnect TOCTOU window a name-only check would leave open.

server.js runs outside the Metro/Expo bundle as plain CommonJS and cannot import frontend/mcm-app/src/bff-server modules directly, so the backup feature's scheduling clock (a setInterval in server.js) reaches the scheduling logic via a loopback HTTP POST to /bff-api/backups/tick guarded by a shared secret (BACKUP_TICK_SECRET), rather than by calling a function; this tick never fires under `pnpm start` because server.js does not run under Metro.

mongo-client.ts explicitly passes a static `runtimeAdapters: { os }` (imported via `import * as os from 'node:os'`) to the MongoClient constructor to work around a mongodb driver ≥7.6.0 regression where the driver's dynamic `import('os')` promise rejects under Jest's CJS runtime and is silently swallowed, collapsing the client metadata document to `{}` and causing MongoDB to refuse the handshake with a 'Missing required sub-document driver' error that mimics a driver/server incompatibility.

The Redis leader lock guarding the scheduled-backup tick (redis-lock.ts) is only an optimisation to avoid duplicate scanning across multiple BFF instances and relies on a TTL guess, so an overrunning run can legitimately lose the lock to another instance while still active; the actual exactly-once guarantee for job execution is a single-document atomic findOneAndUpdate claim in backup-job-store.ts that carries no timing assumption.

Account deletion (feature 076) is three routes over one pipeline: POST /bff-api/account/delete-challenge parks a 5-minute, user-keyed pending request and returns only the authorization URL (or, on native, a state plus the parameters the device must send); GET /bff-api/account/delete is the Keycloak callback, which returns a redirect for every outcome; POST on the same path is the native completion, running the same verification and pipeline but answering JSON. There is no DELETE method and no admin variant, and the user id always comes from the validated session rather than the query.

The normative deletion order is published as data: DELETION_STEPS is tearDownUserBackups, deleteCollections, removeAgentConfig, clearTransientState, terminateSessions, logoutIdpSessions, deleteIdentity, so a reordering shows up as a diff on a named list rather than a quiet edit inside a function body, and account-deletion-order.test.ts asserts against it.

Three constraints carry the deletion order: tearDownUserBackups runs first and already revokes the offline token at the identity provider before deleting any local record, throwing having deleted nothing if the revocation fails; the agent-config document is removed only after the teardown because the standing permission is stored inside it as offlineRefreshEnc; and deleteIdentity runs last because it is the only irreversible step, after which nothing that needed the user to exist can be retried.

runAccountDeletion throws on the first failing step having attempted nothing after it, so the caller reports the account as not deleted rather than a partial success and a retry starts again from the teardown; each step runs through a wrapper recording the failed step by its enumerated name so no downstream message reaches the audit stream; the step-up refresh token is revoked in a finally on the failure path too, so a failed deletion does not leave a second live token set for a still-existing account; and the callback runs to completion even if the client goes away, because nothing wires an inbound abort signal into a cancellation path.

account-deletion.ts must never construct a destination driver and must never import backup-destination-driver, backup-retention, or the driver/store/restore modules, so no code path in account deletion is capable of touching the user's stored artifacts (which are their property at storage they own and pay for). account-deletion-no-driver.test.ts enforces this as a static import assertion rather than a behavioural test, because reading the imports shows the capability is absent entirely while a behavioural test could only show one path did not touch storage on one run.

The collection-deletion step acts with the step-up access token rather than the session's — the step-up token was minted seconds ago and cannot be near expiry, whereas the session's may be after a login form and TOTP prompt — and it treats a 404 from mc-service as success, because a retry after a partial failure re-issues deletes for collections the first attempt already removed and treating that as an error would make the retry fail where it had otherwise worked. Ownership is enforced by mc-service's DAC layer, so the loop cannot reach another user's collection.

The deletion callback is gated on step-up re-authentication that sends the user back to the identity provider rather than collecting a password in-app, because the constitution forbids the application handling credentials and the app client has directAccessGrantsEnabled false so the password grant is unavailable; the authorize request sends prompt=login and max_age=0 together (measured with a control leg: authorize without max_age returns a code with no prompt because the SSO session is reused, authorize with max_age=0 serves the login form again) and asks for scope=openid only, deliberately not offline_access.

Keycloak does not emit amr for this client, so auth_time carries the whole step-up requirement: verification refuses a token with no auth_time (a separate presence check that comes first, so a missing claim never reads as satisfied) and then applies two freshness tests — the proof must be within STEP_UP_MAX_AGE_SECONDS (300, the same constant as the parked record's TTL so the two cannot drift) and strictly greater than the session's own auth_time floor, which is the session's auth_time rather than a wall clock so both values come from Keycloak.

The PKCE verifier is parked server-side on web — state, verifier and redirect URI in Redis keyed by the authenticated user, with only the authorization URL returned to the browser — because a verifier the browser holds is one an attacker holding the authorization code can also use; on native the device runs the flow and expo-auth-session mints the verifier, while the BFF still mints and parks the state as the CSRF binding and single-use marker. A pending record not marked native never reads client-supplied verifier or redirect-URI values, so a web caller cannot opt itself onto the weaker binding.

redirectUri must be identical on both OAuth legs — the authorize request and the code exchange — or Keycloak rejects the exchange with invalid_grant, so it is derived from the origin the request actually arrived on at challenge time and stored with the pending record rather than recomputed on the callback; deriving it from the request is safe against a forged Host because Keycloak only honours redirect URIs registered on the client.

The parked step-up record is consumed before validation whatever the outcome, so a proof that fails its checks is not retryable against the same request and an attacker reaching the callback gets no repeated attempts at the state value; refusals are enumerated as no_pending, state_mismatch, subject_mismatch, missing_auth_time and stale_auth rather than free text, so a refusal can be counted and no message from Keycloak leaks into the audit stream.

The deletion challenge is rate-limited per client IP at 5 requests per hour (skipped with a warning when no trusted client identity can be established), and a user who is the last remaining mc-admin is refused with a 409 before anything is parked.

Because the BFF's Mongo is a standalone mongod with no multi-document transaction, the backup teardown cannot wrap its deletes in one transaction: destinations, jobs and runs are removed as three independent deleteMany calls, ordered destinations → jobs → runs so a crash part-way through never leaves a job pointing at a destination that is gone.

The web security-header layer is a pure plain-CommonJS module (web-security-headers.js) that server.js requires at container boot because the hand-written adapter cannot import the app's compiled TypeScript. It sets X-Frame-Options DENY, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff and Referrer-Policy no-referrer on static assets, SSR HTML and the API surface alike; path-scopes the web CSP out of /bff-api so the API keeps its own strict default-src 'none' CSP as the only CSP present; reads the browser-facing Keycloak origin from env rather than hard-coding it, falling back to the dev default on a malformed, scheme-less or non-web-scheme value (which the WHATWG URL parser would otherwise reduce to the opaque origin string null); and allow-lists Expo Router's one inline bootstrap script by sha256 hash instead of permitting 'unsafe-inline'.

server.js disables X-Powered-By and stamps an X-BFF-Source marker on every response so the web E2E can positively prove the request path is this container rather than the Metro dev server, defeating a silent false-green.

The internal scheduling tick route answers 404 rather than 401 to a wrong secret so it never advertises its own existence, and compares in constant time with the lengths checked first so a length mismatch falls through to the same 404; on the server.js side the interval timer is unref'd, starts after app.listen so the first tick cannot race the port it calls, logs and swallows a failing tick, and is disabled with a single boot-time log line when BACKUP_TICK_SECRET is unset or BACKUP_TICK_INTERVAL_MS is invalid.

The backups routes do not repeat the requireAuth-then-RBAC prologue by hand: withBackupRoute() in backup-route-support.ts runs the request context, requireAuth(), requireMcUser() and the error translation once and passes the handler body an already-authenticated { userId, jwt }, so a backups handler cannot be written without authorization; it also owns the 404-for-not-yours rule (a 403 would confirm the resource exists) and the strict discriminated-union Zod schemas that reject a spoofed userId in the body with a 400.

tests/integration/route-coverage-map.ts and route-coverage.integration.test.ts enforce endpoint coverage structurally: the test globs the live src/app/bff-api/**/+api.ts inventory and fails CI when a route file has neither an integration test nor a written exclusion, when a mapped test file is missing on disk, or when a stale matrix entry names a route that no longer exists; the auth/login code-exchange endpoint is the single permitted exclusion and the gate asserts it is the only one.

GET /bff-api/auth/init is the redirect-URI reconciliation route: it is unauthenticated by design, is called once on app mount best-effort by the client root layout (fetch('/bff-api/auth/init').catch(() => {})), and passes ensureClientRedirectUris() the complete six-entry list this client needs — the web PKCE callback, the verified-email redirect, the native login scheme URI, the backup-consent callback, the account-deletion step-up callback and its own native scheme URI. Because the underlying write is additive and one-shot per process, the list is the contract: a URI left out is never registered by this path, and on a fresh realm nothing fails at deploy time until someone hits that flow.

Three auth cookies cross the wire and nothing else: the access token and session id are scoped to Path=/ while the refresh token is scoped to Path=/bff-api/auth/refresh only, which is what makes it unreachable from an ordinary API request; all three are HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict and Secure outside development, and the clear-cookie set mirrors those attributes exactly because a browser may decline a clear whose attributes do not match the cookie being removed.

Registration is gated by the application-level allowSelfRegistration setting read server-side before any user creation rather than by the realm's self-service flag, because users are created through the Keycloak Admin API; it fails closed on a store error so registration is refused rather than silently allowed, and /register is rate-limited per email and per source IP so varying the email cannot buy unlimited registrations from one source.

POST /bff-api/auth/logout terminates only the caller's own session: the handler authenticates first and acts on the session id only when the session record's userId equals the authenticated subject, so an unauthenticated request carrying a victim's X-Session-Id cannot force-logout them; refresh-token revocation and IAM-level SSO termination (logoutUserSessions) then run only for that authenticated owner.

error-handler.ts (handleBffError) is the older Express-shaped error mapper and is now reachable only from its own unit test: no live route handler imports it (register+api.ts mentions it only in a comment about adapting it), and the live handlers answer with securityHeaders() plus either handleMcApiError() or the RFC 9457-shaped problemResponse()/problem() helpers.

The backup destination protocols sit behind one policy-free interface, BackupDestinationDriver (put/get/list/delete/testConnection, with no bucket, ETag, multipart or storage-class concept), and a driver never receives a URL: createBackupDriver() runs the resolving SSRF guard and builds a PinnedTransport whose agent can only resolve to vetted addresses, so there is no code path from a destination document to a socket that skips the check. createBackupDriver() is also the only place a destination's type is switched on, which is what contains the hand-written SigV4 decision to backup-request-signer.ts and backup-driver-s3.ts.

The BFF ships its own AWS Signature Version 4 signer rather than @aws-sdk/client-s3 (ratified by the operator on 2026-09-20 on supply-chain grounds — the SDK pulls roughly fifty transitive packages for the four operations this feature needs), covering SigV4 only with no chunked/streaming payloads and no presigning; it is verified against two independent external oracles, AWS's published vectors vendored under src/bff-server/unit-tests/fixtures/aws-sigv4/ (which assert the canonical request, the string-to-sign and the authorization header at all three intermediate stages) and backup-driver-s3.integration.test.ts against a real S3-compatible object store, because a signer checked only against its own expectations passes while producing a consistently wrong signature.

The signer's subtle rules are the ones that fail as an opaque signature mismatch rather than a diagnosable error: RFC 3986 encoding that escapes !*'() where encodeURIComponent does not; canonical URI built by encoding each path segment with the separators left alone; the canonical query sorted by encoded key then encoded value (sorting by decoded key is the subtly wrong version that AWS's get-vanilla-query-order-encoded vector exists to catch); and x-amz-date and x-amz-content-sha256 added by the signer itself so they fall inside SignedHeaders rather than being added at the transport layer afterwards.

The S3 driver sends exactly the headers the signer signed (adding one at the transport layer would make the signature cover a different header set than the one on the wire), pages LIST with a continuation token rather than reading only the first response — a first-page-only driver silently under-reports past the 1000-key limit and retention then never prunes below it while reporting success — and never echoes an upstream S3 error document or a credential into a failure reason, exposing only the status and the S3 error Code.

The S3 driver's testConnection separates the three failures that have three different fixes — unreachable, credentials-rejected, and authenticated-but-not-permitted — and then performs a write probe (PUT of a .mcm-write-probe object, best-effort DELETE afterwards) because a read-only key that passes a read-only probe and then fails every backup is precisely the outcome the probe exists to prevent; a transport-level throw is reported as unreachable without echoing the underlying message, which can carry an address or a certificate subject.

The backup integration suites escalate rather than skip quietly: tests/integration/helpers/backup-targets.ts treats missing destinations as a loud SKIP when MCM_REQUIRE_BACKUP_TARGETS is unset but as a HARD FAILURE at a named assertion (assertBackupTargetsPresent) when it is set, so a suite that passes with the targets down is not possible under the flag; the rule for reading a result is therefore to watch the skip count, not the exit code.

The scheduling tick route's contract is deliberately narrow beyond the secret check: the ?now= time override is deny-by-default (400 unless BACKUP_TICK_ALLOW_TIME_OVERRIDE=1, a dev/CI-only flag, because with the tick secret alone any caller could otherwise assert that every schedule is due), due jobs run sequentially rather than concurrently (each run holds its whole artifact in memory, so running them together would create the memory spike the size ceiling exists to prevent), nextRunAt is recomputed forward from now and the claim released in a finally, and the due-filter's $type: 'string' check is load-bearing because MongoDB's cross-type ordering sorts null before every string and a bare $lte would make every on-demand-only job read as permanently due.

A scheduled backup run mints the user's own access token first and a failed mint ends it: runScheduledBackup catches OfflineTokenUnusableError, records a FAILED run carrying the error's user-facing remedy message, and returns without reading or writing anything or trying another identity — there is no service-account path to fall back to, because a backup that quietly succeeded using broader privilege than the user granted would be worse than one that failed.

A backup run holds the whole artifact in memory and writes exactly one object, checking both ceilings before anything is written; the ceiling error names both the limit and the measured value because it is the only guidance an operator gets, and pruning happens only after the PUT returns so a failure leaves no object and the user is never down a version with no replacement.
